processing: A blend of two dried ingredients: safflower petals, called gurgum, and root bark of Cinnamomum tamala, called shing-tsha, which gives most of the flavour.
harvest_season: Little is documented about when the ingredients are gathered.
appearance_dry: Orange-red safflower petals mixed with pieces of brown bark.
appearance_liquor: Golden to orange, as is usual for a safflower infusion.
appearance_wet: Soft, deepened red petals and darkened bark.
taste_profile: Described as having a slightly oily feel; the cinnamon-family bark should give a warm, spiced note over the mild floral safflower, though detailed tasting records are scarce.

brewing.notes: Steep like other herbal infusions, covered, with near-boiling water.

vintage_note: Sold as a dried herbal blend without vintages. As with other herbal blends, buy recent stock and judge by the colour of the petals and the smell of the bark.
description:
Tsheringma is a Bhutanese herbal tea, named after the local goddess of longevity, wealth and prosperity. It contains no tea leaf, just safflower petals and the root bark of a Himalayan cinnamon relative.

The recipe is short. The petals, called gurgum, bring colour; the bark, shing-tsha, brings the flavour and is the part that makes it taste of something.

It is said to feel slightly oily in the mouth. Exact brewing is little documented, so treat it as you would any bark and petal infusion: hot water, a lid and a few minutes.

In Bhutan it is taken as traditional medicine. Healers credit it with calming the nerves and helping the heart, liver and digestion; those are traditional beliefs, not established results. Enjoy it as a taste of the place.
history: Little is documented about when the blend first appeared. It is known as part of Bhutanese traditional medicine and takes its name from the goddess Tsheringma, but its age and the person or institution behind any modern commercial version are not clearly recorded.
